O.outcome_detail: participation in work-based learning

cells.quote: Though the district intends to expand access to WBL, the vast majority of WBL participants have so far been CTE students whose participation was embedded into their CTE programming.
cells.note: The study reports a distribution of WBL participants, not a causal effect or printed effect size.

O.outcome_detail: weekly aggregated number of completed workplace-based assessments

cells.quote: "In nearly all blocks across all years there are more assessments completed in secondary care, especially when secondary care is the first placement block, and early in the placement more generally."
cells.note: The quoted finding is from the wiki entry because the supplied study text does not include the results sentence reporting the direction. The study text describes Year 1 students, clinical skills WBA, and placement blocks lasting 8–10 weeks.

O.outcome_detail: perceived changes in skills, attitudes, behaviour, or willingness to apply knowledge and skills

cells.quote: They all showed a modification of skills and attitudes or behavioural or willingness of learners to apply new knowledge & skills (Kirkpatrick Levels 2 and 3) [6].
cells.note: The review synthesized heterogeneous, non-comparative observational and qualitative studies; the positive result was primarily perceived or self-reported rather than demonstrated against a control condition.

O.outcome_detail: improvement in learning and performance as a direct result of workplace-based assessment

cells.quote: None of the studies showed an improvement in learning and performance as a direct result of WBA (Kirkpatrick Level 4).
cells.note: This reports absence of demonstrated Level 4 evidence, not an adequately powered null effect; all included studies were non-comparative.

D.treatment: well-implemented feedback from workplace-based assessments, particularly multisource feedback
D.comparison: no feedback or comparison not reported

O.outcome_detail: perceived positive effect on clinical practice

cells.quote: There is, however, good evidence that if well implemented, feedback from workplace based assessments, particularly multisource feedback, leads to a perceived positive effect on practice.
cells.note: The review included no randomized trials; the reported benefit was perceived and based on prospective, non-comparative observational or descriptive studies.

D.treatment: textual feedback with large free-text boxes (TAB)
D.comparison: numerical-scale feedback with limited comment space (mini-PAT)

O.outcome_detail: perceived usefulness of feedback

cells.quote: There were small but significant preferences for textual feedback, shown by the team assessment of behaviour (TAB), which has large free-text boxes, being perceived as more useful than the mini-PAT, which has a numerical scale and only a small space for comments.
cells.note: This was a questionnaire-based comparison of perceived usefulness, not a randomized intervention.

D.comparison: global judgments or vague, non-actionable feedback

O.outcome_detail: feedback usefulness and potential for practice improvement

cells.quote: The desirable characteristics of feedback were found to be specificity, behavioural focus, and sufficient clarity to be of great potential value to trainees.
cells.note: The review synthesized observational and qualitative evidence; this contrast concerns the reported characteristics of useful feedback rather than a controlled treatment comparison.

D.treatment: specific feedback, particularly direct patient feedback addressing communication skills
D.comparison: less-specific feedback from medical colleagues addressing clinical competence

O.outcome_detail: self-reported behaviour change or use of feedback in practice

cells.quote: The feedback most consistently used was specific, received from patients, and addressed communication skills. The feedback least frequently used addressed clinical competence and came from medical colleagues.
cells.note: This finding came from qualitative studies of doctors' reported use of multisource feedback; it does not establish a causal effect on objectively measured performance.

cells.quote: ‘T’ test of table.2 indicated that higher secondary level chemistry students of control group (N=24) and experimental group (N=24) differ significantly in the post–test mean scores at 0.01 level of significance.
cells.note: The table reports a higher experimental-group mean, although the following prose incorrectly says that the experimental mean is less than the control mean.

cells.quote: There is no significant difference in the mean score between girls and boys higher secondary students in the Post-test.
cells.note: The article nevertheless states that male students performed better; the reported gender difference is not statistically significant.

The post-test mean score of experimental group (M=20.25) is less than that of the post – test mean score of control group (M=18.33).

O.outcome_detail: mini-CEX overall score

cells.quote: The mini-CEX overall score improved from 6.4 ± 0.8 at baseline to 6.7 ± 0.8 at the end of rotation (P = 0.006).
cells.note: The intervention cohort comprised radiation oncology postgraduates with median previous radiation-oncology exposure of 1 month.

result.effect: Cohen's d = 0.36; mean change = 1.30 (95% CI 0.35 to 2.25)
